dimensions.note: Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. This model handles FOUR distinct bearer credentials — more than any other in the suite — and that is the reason this dimension got the most attention. (1) applicationKey: .meta({ sensitive: true }), vault-sourced, never echoed. (2) The 24h account authorizationToken: header only. (3) The per-endpoint upload token from b2_get_upload_url / b2_get_upload_part_url: postBytes deliberately bypasses the shared client because upload endpoints are off-cluster, carry their own token and take a byte body; the token is set as an Authorization header and never persisted. (4) The download authorization token, which is the design decision worth recording: b2_get_download_authorization returns a token granting read access to a whole prefix for up to seven days, and it is NEVER written to a snapshot or a log. That diverges from b2-key's secretDestination pattern on purpose, and the difference is regenerability — B2 returns an application key's secret exactly once and it is lost forever if uncaptured, whereas this token can be re-minted at will, so persisting a copy would be all risk and no benefit. The guarantee is asserted in the data itself via tokenPersisted: false, not only in prose. Verified by execution across every method: the mechanical harness plants all four secrets in its fixtures and greps every snapshot and log line (step 5, OK), and a dedicated test asserts the account token never travels in a request body. Residual, documented: fileInfo is arbitrary user metadata B2 stores and returns on every read, so it lands in a snapshot verbatim — the README warns it must never hold a credential, matching the bucketInfo precedent.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Structured throughout: message templates with named placeholders and a props object, never concatenated values. Warnings are reserved for facts an operator must not miss and each names the consequence rather than the symptom — a truncated part listing says the counts are a FLOOR, a bucket with no readable bucketId says that is not evidence it has no unfinished uploads, and a rejected download authorization says the token grants nothing. The sharpest one is in the large-upload rescue path: if the upload fails AND the compensating cancel also fails, the warning states that the parts are still stored and still billed and prints the exact command to clean them up, because that is a permanent invisible charge and a generic error would leave the operator with no idea it happened. Asserted by test, not by inspection.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. b2Fetch throws Error & { status, b2Code } and the model branches on the code, never on message text; postBytes reproduces that contract for the upload endpoints so a caller cannot tell which client threw. 401 unauthorized is deliberately not retried — a missing capability is not transient, and the README maps every method to the capabilities it needs. Ordering was audited method by method and the guards fire before any B2 call: the size guard runs before b2_authorize_account itself (which is class-C), and delete's destruction gate runs before authorizing too, both asserted by tests checking calls.length === 0. The compensating-transaction path is the substance here: a large upload that fails after b2_start_large_file leaves a file whose parts are billed indefinitely and are invisible in the console's file browser, so the model cancels it on failure — best-effort, in a nested try, so a failed cancel can never mask the original error. Both branches are tested.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. 55 tests plus a mechanical harness that executes every method and diffs each spec's schema keys against the keys written (14/14, 13/13, 8/8, ALL PASS). CONVENTIONS §10 items 1-7 all covered. Proven to bite by mutation twice (a wrong type on a derived field; a schema-legal sha1Verified ?? false collapsing 'not checked' into 'checked and wrong'), both reverted and re-verified green. Three tests were themselves found wrong and fixed during the build — one asserting on a ReadableStream's start() callback, which fires at construction and so would have passed even if the body HAD been read; one asserting B2's DOCUMENTED already-gone codes rather than the one it actually returns; and the copy_part suite, which tested an argument shape no caller could ever satisfy. That last is the lesson of this dimension: mock tests validate that the code does what the test author believed, and every one of these defects lived in the gap between that belief and B2. All of them were found by RUNNING the thing. The write path is now exercised end to end against real B2 — small upload with SHA-1 verification, large multi-part upload from a local file, download by id and by name, a byte-for-byte round-trip comparison, a minted-and-verified download authorization, server-side assembly from two source ranges verified byte-for-byte against a locally-built expectation, ten real cancels and a repeat cancel — all in a scratch bucket created and destroyed for the purpose.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. scan, download, list_parts and authorize_download are read-only and repeatable. delete is idempotent — and the reason it is has been REWRITTEN after live verification proved the original reasoning wrong. Cancelling an already-cancelled large file does NOT return 404, file_not_present or no_such_file, as B2's error table implies and as the first implementation assumed. It returns the catch-all bad_request with the message 'No active upload for large file (4_z...)'. The original isAlreadyGone therefore rethrew, and delete was not idempotent at all; the mock fixtures asserted the documented codes, so every test agreed with the code while both were wrong about the world. Found by cancelling ten real uploads and then re-running one. The fix required knowingly breaking CONVENTIONS §2's 'branch on the code, never on prose' rule, because bad_request is genuinely non-discriminating and §4.7 already warns that swallowing it wholesale would hide malformed-request bugs. So the match requires the code AND /no active upload for large file/i, and a test asserts that a DIFFERENT bad_request still throws — that second assertion is what keeps a narrow match from decaying into a blanket swallow. The considered alternative, verifying existence first via b2_list_unfinished_large_files (the b2_delete_key precedent), was rejected because that call is addressed by bucket and would spend a class-C transaction on every delete while reintroducing the bucket lookup this method deliberately avoids. isAlreadyGone still excludes bad_bucket_id. Recorded in CONVENTIONS §4 item 10. upload is not idempotent by nature and is documented as such.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Built against the v4 corrections in CONVENTIONS §4 rather than Backblaze's prose. The canonical client (§5) was copied byte-identical from b2-files and verified so programmatically. All thirteen operations are covered and confirmed present by mechanical grep. Two contract details recorded earlier stand: b2_upload_file and b2_upload_part are reached via the uploadUrl B2 returns rather than by name on the cluster apiUrl, and b2_list_parts is scoped by B2 to writeFiles rather than a read capability. Two more were established by live exercise. First, b2_cancel_large_file on an already-cancelled file returns the catch-all bad_request with 'No active upload for large file (...)', not 404 or file_not_present (CONVENTIONS §4.10). Second, b2_copy_part requires an in-progress large file and rejects a completed one with 'No active upload for' — which is what proved the original copy_part signature unusable. Everything is now live-verified against a real account: the read paths on the production fleet, and every write path in a purpose-built scratch bucket, including a server-side assembly whose output was compared byte-for-byte against a locally constructed expectation.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Three specs, cleanly separated by what they describe: unfinished-upload is an object B2 is billing for, transfer is the outcome of one movement, download-auth is a grant's shape. scan is a genuine factory — one execution fans out across every visible bucket and acquires the per-model lock once (CLAUDE.md rule 6). Cost is designed against: countParts is opt-in precisely because it is one class-C call per unfinished file; a pinned bucketName+bucketId skips b2_list_buckets entirely; and the large-upload path fetches b2_get_upload_part_url ONCE and reuses it across parts rather than paying a class-C call per part, asserted by test. The defining decision is the size guard: maxTransferBytes defaults to 100 MB, is checked before any B2 call including authorize, is overridable per run, and is additionally policed by a check that rejects a model-level cap above 1 GiB. A model that can stream a 40 GB restic pack file through a Deno process by accident has no business existing next to this estate; this one cannot.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Every fixture and README example uses example.com-class names and fake-but-plausible B2 identifiers (example-backup-bucket, 4a48fe8875c6214145260818, 4_zexamplelargefileid00001). Checked with particular care because this build read live output containing real bucket names, real Time Machine file paths and real 83-character file IDs — the exact circumstance in which one gets pasted into a fixture, and a mistake I made in this same session in the b2-hygiene README. The model source, the test file, the mechanical harness and the README contain no real bucket name, file path or file ID. The one real-world detail that IS published is the STRUCTURE of a B2 large-file ID (4_z<bucket>_f<file>_d<date>_m<minute>_c<cluster>_v<vol>_t<seq>), which appears in a code comment and a test because it is the justification for the instance-name hash; that is a public property of B2's ID format, not of this account, and the test's fixture IDs are synthetic.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Calibrated per CONVENTIONS §4.9 — strict where the shape is documented and observed, permissive where it is not. Byte and count fields are z.number().int(). The honest-null contract is enforced in the schema itself and its descriptions say what null MEANS, not merely that it is allowed: partCount null is 'not measured, run list_parts', never zero parts; sha1Verified null is 'NOT CHECKED', explicitly distinguished from false meaning 'computed and mismatched'. That three-state distinction is the one most likely to be flattened by a consumer, so the README tells readers to branch on === false rather than on falsiness. contentSha1 is recorded VERBATIM rather than normalised, because B2's 'none' and 'unverified:' prefixes are themselves the fact. tokenPersisted is z.literal(false) — a schema-level guarantee that the field can never carry anything else. fileInfo is held loosely (a non-object degrades to null) so an unexpected shape cannot sink a fleet scan. Field coverage is verified by execution, 1:1 in both directions across all three specs.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. All three specs are lifetime 'infinite' with garbageCollection 50, matching the rest of the suite. Right for unfinished-upload, whose value is the trend — 50 versions of a per-upload part count is the series showing whether an abandoned upload is growing or was finally cancelled, and the delete tombstone needs to outlive the object it describes. Right for transfer, where a canary written on a schedule produces exactly the history you want: 50 round-trips with their SHA-1 verdicts is a readable record of whether a bucket has stayed healthy. For download-auth the cap is close to moot: each (bucket, prefix) pair keys one instance and re-minting rewrites it, so 50 versions is 50 mints of the same grant, which is a useful audit trail at negligible cost.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Seven methods covering all thirteen operations PRD §4 assigns to this model, mapped one-to-one in the README's method table. Method names follow the PRD rather than the §3 taxonomy, a documented divergence — but delete is named delete precisely so its acknowledgement gate sits in execute where it belongs (see preflight-checks). One method changed shape after live exercise, and the change is a correction rather than a feature: copy_part originally took a largeFileId and a partNumber, mirroring b2_copy_part one-for-one, and was UNREACHABLE. b2_copy_part requires an in-progress large file; upload starts and finishes atomically so its result is a completed file B2 rejects with 'No active upload for', and scan only finds unfinished uploads that already exist. On a healthy account — which this one is, now that the ten abandoned uploads are cancelled — there was no way to obtain a valid largeFileId at all. Verified by trying it against live B2 and getting exactly that rejection. copy_part now owns the whole lifecycle (start, copy each source in order, finish), the same shape upload already uses, and cancels the half-built file on failure so it cannot create the invisible billed waste scan exists to find. Coverage is unchanged — the two extra operations were already covered by upload — and the method went from uncallable to working. Deliberately still out of scope: resuming a partially-completed large upload from a previous run, and the S3-compatible API per PRD §2.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. TWO checks, both labelled policy: credentials-present and transfer-limit-sane. A third, transfer-destruction-acknowledged, was written, shipped into the first live run, and REMOVED — and its removal is the most important safety finding of this build. swamp does not pass method inputs to checks, so it could only ever read globalArgs. That made --input allowTransferDestruction=true invisible to it: the documented per-run acknowledgement was rejected before execute ran, and the check's own error message told the operator to do the exact thing the check made impossible. The consequence was worse than a confusing message. With the per-run path blocked, the ONLY route to cancelling anything was to set allowTransferDestruction: true permanently on the model definition — so a check written to prevent accidental destruction was in practice forcing operators to arm destruction for good. It fired on the safe configuration and passed on the dangerous one. The real gate, assertDestructionAllowed inside execute, sees both the input and the global argument, runs before any B2 call, and is tested on each path; a pre-flight check cannot improve on it here. A regression test now asserts that NO check declares appliesTo: ['delete'], because a code comment alone would not stop this being re-added. Recorded in CONVENTIONS §4 item 11, which also notes that @sntxrr/b2/files carries the same defect in its already-published file-destruction-acknowledged check. transfer-limit-sane remains and still catches the analogous mistake for maxTransferBytes.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Every instance is spec-prefixed per CONVENTIONS §2, since names share one flat storage namespace across specs — asserted mechanically, along with no-clobber-within-one-execution and no use of the reserved literal 'latest'. This dimension carries the build's most important defect, and LIVE DATA is what found it. unfinishedInstanceName originally used safeFragment(fileId, 48) with no hash, on the reasoning that fileId is B2's own identifier and therefore unique. That reasoning is wrong once truncated: a real B2 large-file ID is ~83 characters of the form 4_z<bucket>_f<file>_d<date>_m<minute>_c<cluster>_v<vol>_t<seq>, and 48 characters cuts inside the date — discarding everything that distinguishes two uploads of the same file at different times, so they would reduce to one instance name and silently clobber each other on disk. That is exactly the failure that made b2-bucket's notification snapshot eat its bucket snapshot. NO TEST COULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: the mock fixture used a 25-character ID that never reached the truncation. The mock was SHORTER than reality, the mirror image of wave 2's mocks being RICHER than reality, and the same lesson. Fixed by appending a hash of the full ID, with a regression test using two realistic 83-character IDs that share their first 48 characters — verified to fail when the hash is removed.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Carried from the 2026.08.06.1 review; code for this dimension unchanged since (git log), and not re-reviewed in this delta. Resources are shaped for CEL querying: scalar, introspectable fields rather than nested blobs. The questions this model exists to answer are one predicate each — ageDays > 30 && status == 'present' finds abandoned uploads worth cancelling, partBytes != null && partBytes > 0 finds the ones with measurable cost, and sha1Verified == false (not !sha1Verified) finds genuinely corrupt transfers. The nullable contract is what makes those safe, and the README spells out the trap: a !sha1Verified filter silently sweeps in every never-checked transfer alongside the actually-broken ones, which is the difference between an alert that means something and one that fires constantly. partsTruncated sits beside partCount so a consumer can tell a total from a floor.

Delta review for 2026.10.22.1 (hygiene cards #435/#436). Added a no-op baseline upgrades entry with toVersion 2026.08.06.1, equal to the model version, so the chain's last toVersion matches (registry rule). Verified: push --dry-run with the manifest bumped reports no versionBumpUpgrade warning.
